entry.title: Rediscovering Photography
entry.content:
In I Am Assigning Myself Homework, I said I would write more about random topics that tickle my curiosity. I guess I’ve been a bad student this summer. But I have rediscovered an old passion of mine: photography.

When I was at university, I picked up photography as a hobby and started shooting portraits and events. My first ever camera was a Canon EOS Rebel T7i, or an 800D, as it was called in the UK, where I bought it. It was a great camera to start with. I spent countless hours culling and editing my photos, watching tutorials from photographers I admired, and experimenting with composition and my camera’s settings. As I gained confidence, I upgraded the kit lens to a 17–55mm f/2.8 zoom and the trusty nifty fifty, 50mm f/1.8.

Then life got busy. Moving countries, grad school, starting a new job in a new country. Somewhere along the way, I almost forgot I had a camera

This summer, I went to New York and found myself looking left and right, up and down, and taking photos again, mostly with my phone. It reminded me of why I liked photography in the first place. It makes you more observant. You can find beauty in the mundane. And it’s a great creative outlet for someone like me: there’s a lot to learn on the technical side, but also an unlimited amount of creative freedom.

While I was there, I had to stop by B&H and check out the store. I ended up trading in my DSLR and finally upgrading to a mirrorless camera. I’ve taken it out a few times since, and I’m rediscovering how much I enjoy photography, but I also feel like my taste has changed. I used to chase technically “correct” or conventionally “beautiful” photos: a perfect bokeh or a super sharp subject. Now I’m gravitating more towards street photography, which has led to a new learning experience.

It feels very much in line with il fanciullino: a sense of wonder when experiencing the world and the pleasure of learning to look again. I thought I would find my way back to that through writing, but instead, this summer it happened through a forgotten hobby of mine

I am still retraining my photographer’s eye and experimenting with different ways to edit my photos, but I thought I would share a few recent shots.

Until next time.
entry.summary: Finding my way back to photography and learning to look again.

entry.title: What Is an Em Dash—and When Should I Use One?

link.title: What Is an Em Dash—and When Should I Use One?

entry.content:
The slide above is from a talk by Terence Tao at ICM 2026, called Mathematics in the Age of AI. I like this slide. I find it a little funny, but it also made me think. It seems like using proper punctuation is now sometimes associated with AI. When I see an em dash, I think to myself “oh, this was probably AI-generated!” I even started to remove em dashes from some of my writing to make it look “more human.”

The thing is, I think I actually started to use em dashes because of AI. I just saw em dashes appear in more and more text, so I kind of just picked up how to use them by example. However, I don’t remember ever learning in school how to use one properly. So I thought I should finally learn.

I know that in I Am Assigning Myself Homework, I said I would explore things outside of topics I am familiar with (for example, I would not necessarily explore things in AI), but I also said that I wanted to just follow my curiosity. So, I guess the first post in the quest to hear the voice of il fanciullino a bit louder will be at least adjacent to AI.

What is an em dash?

Before looking it up, I thought “–” was an em dash, but that’s actually an en dash. Turns out the em dash is a bit longer. The following table shows the difference between some of the most commonly used horizontal marks.

Symbol Name Role
- Hyphen Joining words, as in well-made
− Minus sign Subtraction: 7 − 4 = 3
– En dash Ranges: pages 12–18
— Em dash A break or interruption in a sentence

I also remembered that when you write a paper in LaTeX, you can define spacing in terms of an em. It turns out that an em is a unit of typographic measurement. In modern digital typography, one em corresponds to the current type size, e.g., in 12-point type, one em is 12 points.

Traditionally, however, one em was described as the width of a capital M. An en is (typically) half an em (this sentence is fun to say out loud quickly!). One useful mnemonic is that the letter n only has one bump and the letter m has two, so it’s double the length (note that this is just a mnemonic that I find useful and not a typographic rule).

When should I use one?

An em dash is a break that you want to reader to notice, and can also be a substitute for commas, parentheses, a colon, or a semicolon, with some difference in tone.

Let’s look at some examples. A pair of em dashes can set off an aside that deserves more attention than it would receive inside commas or parentheses:

My favorite punctuation mark—which is apparently suspicious now—is the em dash.

A single em dash can introduce an explanation (substituting a colon) or create a sharp turn:

I had finally learned the rule—then I noticed that different style guides disagree.

It can also mark an interruption or an unfinished thought:

“But I thought the em dash was—”

“That was an en dash.”

The Chicago Manual of Style gives a simple piece of advice: “When in doubt, edit them out.” So, I guess in my quest to make my text look less AI-generated, I have been following the Chicago Manual of Style. I have now learned enough to use em dashes on purpose—which probably means I should use fewer of them.
entry.summary: Em dashes, en dashes, and punctuation in the age of AI.

entry.title: I Am Assigning Myself Homework
entry.content:
È dentro noi un fanciullino che non solo ha brividi […] ma lagrime ancora e tripudi suoi.

Quando la nostra età è tuttavia tenera, egli confonde la sua voce con la nostra, e dei due fanciulli che ruzzano e contendono tra loro, e, insieme sempre, temono sperano godono piangono, si sente un palpito solo, uno strillare e un guaire solo. Ma quindi noi cresciamo, ed egli resta piccolo; noi accendiamo negli occhi un nuovo desiderare, ed egli vi tiene fissa la sua antica serena maraviglia.

— Giovanni Pascoli, Il fanciullino

Recently, Giovanni Pascoli, a poet from my high school Italian literature syllabus, came to mind. Pascoli wrote about il fanciullino, the inner child that experiences the world with wonder. As we grow older, his voice becomes harder to hear, but does not disappear. Perhaps, it is simply drowned out by familiarity.

There are so many things around me that seem ordinary just because I’ve gotten used to them. I look into my bathroom mirror in the morning without questioning how it was made. Most forks have four prongs (actually, I just found out they are called tines), but I’m not too sure why. It’s not that I find these questions uninteresting (quite the opposite, actually). It’s just that I do not wake up most mornings wondering about the history of forks and there is no forcing function pushing me to learn about it.

As a child, school was constantly making me learn about things I had not chosen myself. On Monday, I might be reading about the Roman Empire. On Tuesday, I would be asked to explain photosynthesis. By Friday, I would be writing a report about Aristotle.

At the time, this did not always feel like a privilege. At the time, this did not always feel like a privilege. There were deadlines, grades and some pressure that came with every test and every assignment. But there was also something wonderful about being handed a subject and told “go learn enough about this and understand it well enough to explain it.”

You didn’t have to be already interested in the topic. Sometimes a topic was boring, and some other times it led down long rabbit holes. Either way, you would spend some time looking into something you would’ve otherwise walked straight past.

As an adult, I have a lot more freedom to decide what I learn, and yet, a much narrower syllabus. Without a teacher assigning the next chapter, I find it way too easy to remain inside the subjects I am already somewhat familiar with.

So I have decided to start assigning myself homework.

I want to pick questions and spend some time trying to answer them. Then, I want to write about what I learn. I am not trying to become the world’s leading authority on the history of forks. I’m just trying to understand a new topic well enough to write about it.

I want to publish my learnings even if they feel incomplete. Maybe, especially if they feel incomplete. Part of this experiment is exercising the muscle of finishing small things.

I want to spend more time being a beginner. I want to follow questions that are interesting without first requiring them to be important. I want to practice researching and explaining. And I would like to gradually build a small pile of things I once did not know.

Perhaps, somewhere in that process, I will get a little better at hearing il fanciullino again.

This post is, technically, the first assignment: a short essay on why I intend to write essays.

There will be no grades. There might, however, be stickers.
entry.summary: On recovering curiosity by assigning myself homework.

entry.title: The Quantum Cheese Conundrum
entry.content:
Update (2026-08-08)

I thought I would delete this post once I started writing more regularly, but I might keep it around for posterity. I think it’s kind of fun(ky)!

Note

This is a temporary blog post with entirely fictional content for the purpose of testing markdown syntax. Any resemblance to real scientific theories or dairy products is purely coincidental. This blog post is was generated with Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

Introduction

In the realm of quantum gastronomy, few topics have garnered as much attention as the mysterious properties of interdimensional cheese. Our research team, composed of the brightest minds from both the feline and canine scientific communities, has stumbled upon a fascinating phenomenon that could revolutionize our understanding of the universe—and snack time.

The Quantum Cheese Equation

At the heart of our discovery lies the Quantum Cheese Equation:

\[\begin{align} \mathcal{Q}_c = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\rho(t) \cdot \omega^2}{e^{i\theta t} + \sin(\pi t)} dt \end{align}\]

Where:

  • \(\mathcal{Q}_c\) represents the quantum cheesiness factor
  • \(\rho(t)\) is the time-dependent density of dairy quarks
  • \(\omega\) is the angular frequency of lactose oscillations
  • \(\theta\) is the phase angle of curdling

This equation suggests that the quantum properties of cheese are intricately linked to the fabric of spacetime itself.

Flavor Distribution Analysis

Our team conducted extensive taste tests across multiple parallel universes. The results are summarized in the following table:

Universe Cheddar Sharpness Mozzarella Stretchiness Brie Pungency
Alpha-1 7.2 9.8 3.5
Beta-3 4.6 12.3 8.9
Gamma-7 11.5 6.2 5.7
Delta-9 9.1 8.7 7.2

These findings suggest a correlation between universal constants and cheese characteristics, leading us to formulate the Theorem of Temporal Cheddar.

The Theorem of Temporal Cheddar

Theorem 1

For any given timeline, the sharpness of cheddar \((S_c)\) is inversely proportional to the curvature of spacetime \((\kappa)\) multiplied by the square root of the universe’s age \((T)\).

\[S_c = \frac{k}{\kappa \sqrt{T}}\]

Where \(k\) is the universal cheese constant, approximately equal to \(3.14159\) wheels per parsec.

To illustrate this theorem, we present Figure 1:

Figure 1: Parmigiano-Reggiano, a cheese known for its sharpness and temporal stability.

Implementing the Cheese-Time Algorithm

To further explore the implications of our discoveries, we developed a Python script to simulate the behavior of quantum cheese across dimensions:

import numpy as np

def quantum_cheese_simulator(universes, cheese_types):
    cheese_matrix = np.random.rand(universes, cheese_types)
    
    for i in range(universes):
        for j in range(cheese_types):
            cheese_matrix[i, j] *= np.sin(i * j * np.pi / cheese_types)
    
    return cheese_matrix

# Simulate 10 universes with 5 cheese types each
result = quantum_cheese_simulator(10, 5)
print("Quantum Cheese Distribution:")
print(result)

This code generates a matrix representing the quantum cheese distribution across multiple universes, taking into account the oscillating nature of dairy quarks.

Conclusion

While our research is still in its early stages, the implications are clear: cheese is not just a delicious snack, but a fundamental building block of the multiverse. Future studies will focus on harnessing the power of quantum cheese for time travel and interdimensional communication.

Remember, in science as in cheese, it’s important to keep an open mind and a willing palate. Stay tuned for our next paper: “Schrodinger’s Cheese: Simultaneously Moldy and Fresh Until Observed.”

This is the end of the temporary blog post. Let’s make this a bit longer just because. This is then end!
entry.summary: An exploration of interdimensional dairy products and their impact on the space-time continuum.
